newsitem.title: INDIA: India economic growth seen falling short of target.
newsitem.headline: India economic growth seen falling short of target.

text.p: High interest rates and infrastructure bottlenecks are expected to prevent India from meeting its economic growth target this year, economists said on Wednesday.
The government has set a goal of 6.6 percent growth in gross domestic product (GDP) in the 1996/97 fiscal year that began on April 1. In 1995/96, GDP grew by 7.0 percent.
But economists said the government may be over-optimistic.

"Infrastructure bottlenecks and high interest rates are factors slowing growth," Shashanka Bhide, an economist at National Council of Applied Economic Research told Reuters. Bhide forecast 6.0 percent growth this year.
Trends in industrial growth, trade, the stock market and corporate earnings paint a picture of a slowing economy, analysts said.
"We have been expecting a slowdown in GDP. We expect a growth of 5.5 percent," said Subra Subramanain of H.G. (India) Securities.

Industrial growth is lagging behind the government's 12 percent target, analysts said. "It is difficult to achieve the target of industrial growth of 12 percent," V. Raghuraman, secretary general of the Associated Chambers of Commerce (Assocham), told Reuters.
Industrial growth was 12 percent in 1995/96. Growth in the first two months of the 1996/97 fiscal was 9.9 percent compared to the same period last year, Industry Ministry figures show.
Raghuram said tight liquidity along with high interest rates and a sluggish capital market would strap industry.
The Reserve Bank of India has said it expects interest rates to fall in coming months. A decline in the cost of money would spur investment and industrial growth, analysts said.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram met central bank governor C. Rangarajan on Monday to discuss credit policy, to be announced next month.
Chidamabaram was quoted on Wednesday by local newspapers as saying it was too early to predict a slowdown.
But infrastructure bottlenecks could prove to be the economy's Achilles' heel, anlaysts said.

Chidamaram has admitted that sluggish output this year in six key infrastructure sectors -- power, crude oil, steel, oil products, cement and coal -- could dash the government's hopes of achieving its growth target.
Between April and August, production in those six sectors increased by 3.5 percent compared to 11.7 percent during the same period in 1995.

India's exports between April and July grew 11.45 percent compared to 29.86 percent in the same period last year. Imports in that period fell 5.95 percent compared to a 39.20-percent increase last year.
"There is an import compression, which reflects a slowdown in industrial growth," Raghuraman said. "Both imports and exports have also slowed," he said.
Said Bhide: "Services, to the extent it is related to production and trade, would also slow down."
The silver lining was stronger than expected in agricultural production and a spurt in foreign direct investment proposals cleared by the government.
Subramanian said agricultural output was expected to rise by 2.0 percent in 1996/97, double the 1.0 percent target.
Foreign direct investment, which is crucial to infrastructure growth and totaled some $2 billion in 1995/96, is expected to double this year, he said.
